zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 ([source](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); [license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)). The diplomatic readings and English notes in this return are scan-based review work, not a reproduction of that index.

lines.note: Kenge is explained as satori wo hiraku, opening or attaining understanding. The Portuguese begins 'knowing and understanding', continued in the Buddhist qualification below.

runs.text: entender bem as couſas do Buppô.

lines.note: The understanding concerns the Buddhist teaching, Buppou. Buppô is an embedded Japanese term in the italic explanation, whereas the final Bup. label is upright; the lowercase types should not be made roman merely because the word is Japanese. The scan supports a circumflex in Buppô rather than the draft's grave accent.
Kengyou has two printed romanizations, joined by Latin l for 'or'. The first definition concerns an office or dignity, with dignidade divided at the edge.

The first dignity belongs to Buddhist clergy of Xǒdo. The scan shows a caron, not a tilde; the draft's mixed treatment is retained, with X roman and the visibly slanted ǒdo italic. A second dignity is introduced for the following description of blind people.

runs.text: nidade que ha entre os cegos polla qual ficão a-

lines.note: This dignity among blind people gives its holders a recognized rank. The printed a- remains at the end of the line before graduados, rather than being absorbed or deleted.
The rank is compared with that of doctors or learned graduates. The row is visibly indented like the surrounding continuations; the draft's flush-left placement is corrected.
Kengeki combines sword and spear, tsurugi and hoko. The Portuguese second weapon follows on the next row.
The example kengeki wo taisuru means carrying sword and spear. The divided Portuguese trazer begins here, and the printed joined taiſuru is retained.
Completes trazer and the instruction to carry both weapons. The final S. is upright, marking written usage.
Kengi is explained as avoiding what is doubtful or suspicious. Kirau is represented by printed qirǒ; the gloss elaborates on legal and reputational caution.

runs.text: afaſtarſe de duuidas como nas demandas, não

lines.note: The gloss describes staying away from doubtful matters, as in lawsuits. Its negative instruction about belief continues on the following row.

runs.text: creer facilmente a quem arrezoa porſi, ou vem

lines.note: One should not readily believe someone pleading his own case or bringing doubtful claims. Historical creer, arrezoa and joined porſi remain as printed.
This finishes the warning about doubtful claims and introduces a second application: guarding against conduct that others could suspect or misconstrue.

runs.text: de fazer couſas que ſe podem tomar em mà-

lines.note: The conduct can be taken in a bad sense. Enlargement shows a grave-like mark over the a in mà-; the printed trailing hyphen is retained although the next word is parte.

runs.text: parte, ou duidar da tenção com que ſe fa-

lines.note: The gloss concerns either interpreting actions badly or doubting their intention. The source prints tenção, not a modernized intenção, and divides fazem at the edge.
Zem completes fazem and the extended definition of kengi. The final S. is a separate roman usage label.
Kengyo is explained as kakaru uo, a fish that gets caught. The Portuguese specifies the means of capture on the next row.
The fish is caught on a hook. This continuation completes the entry and is followed by the upright written-usage label S.
Kengyuu and Shokujo form the stellar pair associated with Tanabata. The scan supplies the caron in the headword and the full italic Vt, correcting the draft's unmarked vowel and V.

runs.text: Duas eſtrelas de que falão os poe-

lines.note: Nabata completes tanabata. The Portuguese describes two stars spoken of by poets, without requiring a modern astronomical identification in the canonical text.

runs.text: tas que eſtão hũa no cabo, & outra no princi-

lines.note: The poets place one star at one end and the other at the beginning of the Milky Way. The damaged initial in hũa is h, not OCR b, and principio continues below.
Completes principio da via lactea and the source's description of the stars' positions. The physical row remains independent despite its brevity.
Ken-i denotes imposing power or authority, with Japanese explanations involving governing and overawing. The internal hyphen separates the vowels and is not a line-break mark.
Der completes poder. Ken-i wo katte begins an example of acting by borrowed authority; the source's catte spelling and attached object particle are preserved.
Gegi wo kuwayuru completes the example of issuing an order with borrowed authority. The doubled uu in cuuayuru is the printed form, not a modernized kuwayuru spelling.
The command relies on somebody else's power and authority. The joined ajudandoſe and dalguem remain source spellings.
Kenin is a servant or household person, explained by ie no hito. The following rows broaden the household connection beyond employment alone.

runs.text: pertence a algũa caſa, ou familia, ou por via

lines.note: The person belongs to a house or family. The construction por via introduces the kinds of relationship specified on the next row.
Membership can arise through kinship or service. This completes the qualification of kenin without collapsing the two relationships into one.
Kenzen is something manifest or evident. The entry is independent despite the short one-line definition.
Kenzetsu is open speech or discourse. The final t is the source's checked-coda notation, and the Portuguese abbreviated adverb continues semantically into the next row.
'Or in public' completes the definition of open speaking. It is an alternative circumstance, not a separate meaning requiring a new entry.
Kenji, kenzuru, kenjita gives principal verb forms for offering or presenting. The abbreviated forms are preserved rather than expanded in the transcription.
Sakazuki wo kenzuru means presenting a sake cup. The object of the Portuguese sentence is carried onto the following row.

Sacazzuqui completes the Portuguese naming phrase and is an embedded Japanese term despite its italic type. The next example concerns offering remonstrance to a superior; the historical amoestar is divided after A-, without an inserted d.

runs.text: moeſtar a peßoa nobre offerecendolhe por eſ-

lines.note: The remonstrance is addressed to a noble person by presenting something in writing. The source's peßoa and joined offerecendolhe are retained, with escrito divided at the edge.
Completes escrito and specifies the matters that the noble person should heed. The written warning is the content of the offered remonstrance.
Kenjin is a wise person, kashikoi hito. Abrasion affects Caxicoi, but the remaining letters and the Portuguese prudente support the retained reading.
The definition adds settled judgment, firmness, constancy and independence. These qualities elaborate the prudent person's character rather than introduce new Japanese terms.
The person is upright in conduct. This completes the character description of kenjin.

runs.text: Certa laya de ferro das frechas, co-

lines.note: Kenjiri names a kind of iron arrowhead. The Portuguese comparison is divided after co- and continues on the next row.
Como ponta de espada compares the arrowhead with a sword point. It describes the shape, not an alternative weapon entry.
This kenjitsu is firm truth, katai makoto. The final S. is the roman written-usage label.
A second kenjitsu means a previous day, kanete no hi. The repeated example starts with the nasal abbreviation Qẽ-, which is preserved rather than expanded.
Kenjitsu yori mousu koto de gozaru refers to something said since earlier days. The scan has final t in jit, correcting the OCR c and its unusable kana hint.

runs.text: que digo des dos dias atras.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the thought as something said from days before. The printed des dos is not silently changed to modern desde os.
This kenjitsu means making truth manifest, makoto wo arawasu. The initial Q and the f of Manifeſtação correct OCR Cenjit and Maniſeſtação respectively.
'Of the truth' completes the manifestation gloss. The upright S. closes the column's final entry.

runs.text: O ver de longe, ou de fora. ¶

lines.note: Kenjo is viewing from afar or from outside. The following example begins with an upright Qẽ-; the nasal abbreviation is Japanese, not italic Portuguese.
Kenjo no hito nanto omowou ka asks what outside observers will think. The Portuguese ends with a comma after vẽ, not the OCR hyphen; the printed prospective spelling vomouôca is retained.

runs.text: ou conſiderão de fora que cuidarão?

lines.note: The Portuguese asks what those who watch or consider from outside will think. Its interrogative completes the preceding Japanese example.

runs.text: Premio que algum ſenhor dà pellos

lines.note: Kenjou is a reward given by a lord. The enlarged capital reads P in Premio, correcting OCR Tremio; the reason for the reward follows below.

runs.text: ſeruiços que lhe fazem. Poſto que na igreja

lines.note: The reward is for services rendered. The gloss then comments on a different form current in church usage, rather than introducing another unrelated definition.

runs.text: uanjǒ. Mas a propria palaura ſe tem

lines.note: Quanjou is reported as the church form, but the dictionary questions it. The scan shows a caron; its capital Q is upright while the following letters share the italic explanation's type.
The preferred form is given as Kenjou, followed by an example about awarding a reward. The quoted form has mixed roman Q and italic following letters, contrasting with the fully roman example.

runs.text: Dar premio como renda, &c. a alguem.

lines.note: The example means granting someone a reward such as income or an estate. Its initial S. is upright and belongs to the preceding Japanese expression's usage apparatus.
Kenjou ni azukaru means receiving a reward. The first letter of azzucaru is a, followed by two z types; this corrects the OCR's three-z beginning.
The reward is alternatively described as payment for service. This completes the receiving-reward example.
Kenmei is staking or risking one's life, inochi ni kakuru. The headword has no true internal word break; the gloss's risk verb has two r types before its line-end division.

runs.text: car a vida por algum lugar, renda, ou terras.

lines.note: Completes arriscar: risking one's life for a position, revenue or land. These are the possible stakes of the act, not new Japanese synonyms.
Issho kenmei no chi is explained as a place acquired at the cost of one's life. The source's comma and joined qenmeino are retained rather than reshaped into modern isshoukenmei.

runs.text: gar que comprei com a vida.

lines.note: Completes lugar and the statement 'a place I bought with my life'. This is the dictionary's interpretation of the preceding land-related expression.
Kenmen combines silk and floss or wadding, kinu and wata. The headword reads Qenmen, without the extra i introduced by OCR Qienmen.
The Portuguese specifies Japanese silk and borra, floss or waste fibre. Iapão is Portuguese and remains italic; the final S. is upright.
Kenmi denotes observing or spying. The example repeats the headword across the physical division Qen-/miuo.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Eſpia que vai ver o

lines.note: Completes kenmi wo suru. The second sense is a scout or spy who goes to see what is happening; the scan supports the word separation ver o.
'What is happening' completes the scout's task. The continuation is part of the Portuguese definition, not a Japanese example.
Kenmitsu contrasts manifestation with concealment, araware and kakururu. Its final t is preserved as the dictionary's checked-coda spelling.
Secrecy completes the contrast. The Bup. abbreviation labels Buddhist usage; here its slanted forms are retained within the italic passage rather than globally regularized to roman.
Kenmon is seeing and hearing, mi and kiku. The paired Japanese verbs correspond directly to the Portuguese infinitives.
A separate kenmon denotes a judge or presiding official. Its identical romanization does not justify merging it with the preceding sensory term.
Kenmon kakuchi introduces external perception and knowledge. The explanatory i is upright; exteriormente is physically divided after exte-.

runs.text: riormente, & ſaber, ou eſpecular por eſtes

lines.note: Completes exteriormente and describes knowing or examining through the two senses just named. The source's eſpecular is retained in its intellectual sense.
The two senses are seeing and hearing. The scan reads ſentidos, correcting OCR ſemtidos; Bup. remains italic here, as in the nearby Buddhist label.
The five sensory terms correspond to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. The printed mi tan lacks a comma between the last two items; the transcription does not supply one.

runs.text: potenciàs de ver, ouuir, cheirar, goſtar, &

lines.note: The Portuguese lists the faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling and tasting, with touch following below. A faint short mark is visible over the a of potenciàs on enlargement, so the draft's grave is retained rather than removed or modernized.

runs.text: palpar. Os objeitos deſtes ſentidos ſão.

lines.note: Touch completes the faculties. The Portuguese then introduces their objects, starting with shiki, visible form; Xiqi is an embedded technical term in that explanatory enumeration.

The remaining objects are sound, smell, taste and touch. The last form is visibly ſocu and is retained without converting it to modern shoku; these terms complete the Portuguese-introduced enumeration.

runs.text: Perigo deſer morto à eſpada. Vt,

lines.note: Kennan here means the danger of being killed by the sword. The joined deſer is retained, and Vt introduces an example of encountering that danger.
Kennan ni au, alternatively kakaru, means encountering danger from a sword. The separator is Latin l, not OCR i; the false space after initial Q is removed.

runs.text: rigo de ſer morto à eſpada.

lines.note: Completes perigo and repeats the risk of death by the sword. This is the preceding example's translation.
A distinct kennan denotes roughness or difficulty, explained by kewashuu and katai. Qeuaxǔ is one Japanese word, not the draft's separated Q euaxǔ.
The adjective is illustrated with kennan na tokoro, a difficult place. Its initial Q belongs to the same word and is not a separate element.
Michi supplies the alternative 'road', introduced by Latin l. The Portuguese describes a bad place or road, with the difficulty of passage completed below.
The place or road is difficult to pass through. Paßar retains the visible ligature-like spelling used in this typeface.
Kennou means respectfully presenting something, with Japanese explanations tatematsuri and osamu. The recipient is supplied in the continuation.
The offering is made to a noble person. The source's nasal abbreviation and peßoa are retained; S. is upright.

runs.text: Veſtido que ſe traz de còte.

lines.note: Ke no fuku is clothing worn habitually or daily. The gloss's historical de còte is preserved rather than replaced by a modern expression.
Kenpaku combines silk and wadding, kinu wata. The Japanese explanation lacks a comma here, unlike some neighbouring paired glosses, and is retained as printed.
The second material is described as cotton or floss. This completes the preceding material-pair definition.
Kenpei refers the reader to Qen. The cross-reference word and final S. are upright; Qen is a Japanese term embedded in the editorial direction Vide.
Kenpyou is hard ice, katai koori. The Portuguese source calls it caramelo here; that word is retained and understood through the Japanese explanation rather than modern confectionery usage.
The ice is also thick. Enlargement resolves the OCR's eſpejo as eſpeßo, with the s-pair shape comparable to nearby peßoa and paßar; finer ligature classification remains a typography caveat.

Kenpou combines sword and spear, tsurugi and hoko. The initial is Q rather than OCR D. Enlargement at the right rule shows a small two-stroke hyphen after lan; it is restored as visible print, not inferred merely because lança continues below.
Ça completes lança. Both letters belong to the italic Portuguese word; the OCR's isolated roman a is removed, while final S. stays upright.

zones.label: Catchword
zones.note: The compact mark over e is read as an abbreviation tilde in Qẽpu, anticipating Qenpu on the next page. Its small, thick form is a nonblocking graphic uncertainty; it has not been expanded in the transcription.
